intro.caption: Lesson 5-6 — nets and surface area. Welcome to Fold-or-Fail Papercraft, Cubeland's wildest game show! Three reader gates and a final fold stand between the crew and the trophy.

balloons.t: Round one: fold a flat net into a closed cube, then find its surface area.
Easy! A cube has six squares, so ANY six squares fold into a cube. Watch!
Hold on, Dree! That straight strip overlaps itself and leaves two ends open!

pages.caption: Counting six squares is not enough. In a true net, the edges must meet cleanly with no overlap and no missing sides.

balloons.t: Fold the pattern in your head. If every face lands on its own side, the net works!
Next round! Look at the 2D faces in each net to name the 3D solid.
When I unfold a box flat, I see all six rectangles. Opposite faces match!
So three pairs of faces! Add all six areas and we get the surface area!
We already folded ours! Your crew is still counting faces on flat paper.
Three locks on the prize vault. Let's fold and solve!
Trophy won! Now can I eat the extra blueprints?

win.caption: A net is a flat two-dimensional pattern that folds into a 3D solid. Add the area of every face in the net to find the surface area.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Test the Nets
gates.prompt: Dree's straight strip failed. Pick the net that folds into a closed cube, then find a cube's surface area.
hints: Conceptual: a cube has 6 square faces, and none can overlap when folded.
Procedural: imagine folding a cross shape up from the center square, then multiply one square's area by 6.

steps: Practice cube: a cross-shaped net has 6 equal squares, 1 in the center, 4 around it, and 1 flap on the end.
worked.q: If a cube net has 6 squares of 3 cm² each, what is its surface area?

items.q: Which flat pattern of 6 squares folds into a closed cube?

options.t: A cross shape (4 squares in a row, 1 on each side)
A straight strip of 6 squares in one line
options.fb: Four squares wrap around the middle, so the 5th and 6th overlap on the same side and leave the ends open.
A 2 × 3 block folds two squares onto the same face and cannot close into a cube.
A cube needs 6 faces, not 5. One side would stay wide open.

items.label: A cube net has 6 equal squares. Each square is 9 cm². Total surface area (cm²):
items.aria: total surface area of cube net in square centimeters

fb.msg: 15 is 6 + 9. Multiply the 6 faces by 9 cm² each.
36 is 4 × 9. A cube net has 6 squares, not 4.
45 is 5 × 9. Don't leave out the 6th square face!

items.fbDefault: Multiply the area of one square (9 cm²) by all 6 faces.

gates.pass: The cross-shaped net snaps into a perfect cube, and 6 × 9 = 54 cm². Dree tosses her floppy strip aside.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Name the Faces
gates.prompt: Look closely at the flat faces in each net to identify the 3D solid it builds.
hints: Conceptual: every flat face on a solid shows up once in its net.
Procedural: count the shapes in the net—squares, rectangles, or triangles—and match them to the solid.

steps: The 2 triangles form the two ends, and the 3 rectangles wrap around the sides.
That folds into a triangular prism with 5 faces.
worked.q: How many faces does a triangular prism net show?

items.q: A net shows 1 square in the center and 4 triangles attached to its edges. What solid does it fold into?

options.fb: A rectangular prism net has 6 rectangles, not 4 triangles.
A triangular prism has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles.
A cube net has 6 equal squares and no triangles.

items.q: A rectangular prism is unfolded into a net. How many faces does it show?

options.fb: Four faces only wrap the sides. You forgot the top and bottom.
Check the opposite face! Every face has a twin, so the count is even.
8 is the number of corners (vertices), not flat faces.

gates.pass: Square pyramid and 6-face prism locked in! Moss high-fives Gel.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Unfold the Box
gates.prompt: Kai unfolded a box net into 6 flat rectangles. Add all 6 faces to find the surface area.
hints: Conceptual: surface area is the total area of all flat faces in the net, in square units.
Procedural: find the 3 different face areas, double each one for its matching twin, and add them.

steps: Practice net: a box 5 in × 3 in × 2 in.
worked.q: What is the surface area of a 4 × 3 × 2 box?

items.label: Box net (6 × 4 × 2 in): 2(6×4) + 2(6×2) + 2(4×2) = (in²):
items.aria: surface area of 6 by 4 by 2 box in square inches

fb.msg: 44 only counts 3 faces. Each face has an opposite twin, so double each pair.
48 is 6 × 4 × 2, which is volume. Surface area adds all 6 flat faces.
You missed the 4 × 2 pair (2 × 8 = 16). Include all three pairs!

items.fbDefault: Compute 2(24) + 2(12) + 2(8) and add all three pairs.

items.q: Why does unfolding a box into a net help you find surface area?

options.t: It lays every face flat so no faces are hidden
It measures how much space fits inside the box
options.fb: Space inside is volume. A net shows the outside faces.

options.t: It turns square units into cubic units
options.fb: Surface area always uses square units because nets are flat 2D faces.

gates.pass: 88 in²! Kai's unfolded box folds right back up without a single missing flap.

gates.title: Boss Gate · The Final Fold
gates.prompt: Three final locks on the prize vault. Match the net, fold the cube, and calculate the crate's surface area.
hints: Conceptual: match the face shapes to the solid, and always include all 6 faces of a cube or box.
Procedural: for a cube, multiply one square's area by 6. For a box, add all 3 doubled pairs.

steps: Practice lock: a cube net has squares of side 5 cm (area 25 cm²).
worked.q: What is the surface area of a 3 × 2 × 1 box?

items.q: Lock 1 · Which net folds into a triangular prism?

options.fb: 6 equal squares fold into a cube, not a triangular prism.
1 square and 4 triangles fold into a square pyramid.
4 triangles fold into a triangular pyramid, not a prism.

items.label: Lock 2 · A cube net has 6 squares, each 7 cm × 7 cm. Surface area (cm²):
items.aria: surface area of cube with 7 cm edges in square centimeters

fb.msg: 49 cm² is only 1 square face. A cube has 6 faces.
196 is 4 × 49. Include the top and bottom too—all 6 squares.
343 is 7 × 7 × 7, which is volume. Surface area is 6 × (7 × 7).

items.fbDefault: Find one square (7 × 7 = 49), then multiply by 6 faces.

items.label: Lock 3 · A crate net is 7 in × 3 in × 2 in. Total surface area (in²):
items.aria: surface area of 7 by 3 by 2 crate in square inches

fb.msg: 41 is only 3 faces. Double each face pair for the 6-face net.
42 is volume (7 × 3 × 2). Add all 6 flat faces instead.
You left out the 3 × 2 pair (2 × 6 = 12). Add all three pairs.

gates.pass: CLICK! The prize vault pops open—294 cm² and 82 in²! The Champs stare as Gel eats the confetti.

journal.heading: Lesson 5-6 — what the papercraft show taught us
rows: A flat 2D pattern that folds into a 3D solid. Six squares only make a cube if their edges meet without overlap.
Cube: 6 equal squares. Rectangular prism: 6 rectangles. Triangular prism: 2 triangles + 3 rectangles. Square pyramid: 1 square + 4 triangles.
Find the area of every flat face in the net and add them all together, using square units.
Counting 6 squares is not enough—a straight 1 × 6 strip overlaps and leaves ends open.
journal.quote: "Fold it in your head before you glue it—and keep flat nets away from Gel." — Ana

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 5-6 (Represent Three-Dimensional Figures in Two Dimensions) as one focused read. Covers only this lesson: valid vs. invalid nets, matching nets to solids, counting faces, and computing surface area by summing net faces.
standards: Find the surface area of right rectangular prisms, right triangular prisms, and pyramids using nets
